Board Technology & Innovation Oversight

…

The thesis

Technology reached the boardroom as a hazard. Regulation put cyber risk on the agenda and boards responded, almost universally. But the reason technology matters to a company is mostly upside: what it lets the firm build, enter, automate and pre-empt. This research asks whether boards have taken ownership of that upside, or only of the downside.

It is answerable from filings, because a board that owns something has to say which body owns it. So rather than ask directors what they believe they govern, the study reads what their companies have committed to in writing: six domains, 20 topics, scored the same way 468 times, every score traceable to a quoted sentence in a 10-K, proxy or committee charter.

The finding…

The maturity scale

Four levels, and one dividing line

Each board is placed at a single level from the structural evidence in its filings. The midpoint is the study's dividing line: the bottom half is a board overseeing technology as a risk, the top half is a board that also reaches decisions about what technology is supposed to create. Hover any level for its full rubric definition.

Each bar is the share of boards that have taken documented ownership somewhere in that domain, at least one topic assigned to a named board body, or actively exercised through a stated cadence or named owner. Mentions without ownership are counted separately, in the lighter band.

Board ownership by domain

Highest level any company reaches within each of the six domains. Read the two darkest bands together as "this board owns some part of this domain"; everything to their right does not.

The shape of the finding

Where the scores actually sit

The headline means hide their own spread. These two views put it back: how far apart the six domains are, and how the risk-minus-value gap is distributed across individual boards rather than averaged into one number.

Risk oversight vs. value creation

Domain mean on the 0–3 topic-scoring scale, with the 90th percentile as the lighter bar. A high p90 against a low mean means a few boards do this and the rest do not.

Risk-oversight domain Value-creation domain 90th percentile

The risk-minus-value gap

Each company's mean across the two risk-oversight domains minus its mean across the four value-creation domains. Positive means the board oversees technology risk more closely than technology value. It is a within-company comparison, so it is not affected by a company simply disclosing less overall.

Cut 01

By sector

Sector is the cut a benchmark is actually for: it lets a board ask whether its own posture is normal for its industry. Sectors with fewer than five companies in the sample are not shown.

Risk oversight and value creation by sector

Domain means on the 0–3 scale, sorted by the size of the gap between them.

Cut 02

By oversight structure

Whether a company runs a dedicated standing technology committee, folds technology into an existing committee such as Audit or Risk, or keeps it at the full board.

Breadth of ownership by structure

Mean number of the 20 topics owned at level 2 or 3.

Structure comparison

Confound, read before quoting this Standing-committee companies also have far higher charter coverage (… vs … for existing-committee companies), because a dedicated committee is the kind that publishes a charter. Part of the apparent advantage is document access, not governance. This comparison should not be published as causal until charter coverage is equalised.
Cut 03

By maturity band

This is the second of the two scales, a single company-level classification on the 1–4 rubric, assigned from structural evidence and entirely separate from the 0–3 topic scoring used everywhere else. It is shown here as a consistency check: if the two instruments measure the same underlying thing, breadth should rise with maturity.

Why level 4 is missing Maturity 4 (Leading) holds too few companies in this sample to report as a band, so it is dropped from this cut along with every other group under five. It is not absent from the scale.
Landscape

Who even has a technology committee

A separate, wider pass over Fortune 500 proxy statements, detecting the presence and type of a board-level technology or innovation committee. This layer answers "what structure exists"; the framework layer answers "what that structure actually oversees".

Adoption by Fortune rank band

Share of scored companies with a confirmed dedicated technology or innovation committee. Adoption varies by 13 points across 500 companies with no rank gradient: committee formation is not tracking company size.

What these committees are called

Committee-name prevalence among confirmed adopters. Names matter: a "Science & Technology" committee and a "Cybersecurity" committee are not doing the same job.

Where the mandatory cybersecurity disclosure actually routes

Since the SEC cybersecurity disclosure rule took effect, every filer must name the board body overseeing cyber risk. That makes routing observable, including for companies that have a technology committee and still send cyber somewhere else.

Finding … This is the clearest evidence in the dataset that a technology committee is often a value or strategy body while risk oversight stays with Audit, or that the committee exists without the mandate following it.

Adopters routing cyber to their own technology committee, by sector

Share of each sector's adopters whose cyber oversight sits with the technology committee rather than Audit or the full board.

01

What is measured

The unit of measurement is documented board ownership, not the quality of oversight, and not the company's technology performance. A board can govern technology superbly and score low here if it does not say so in a filing. The instrument is deliberately conservative: it scores only what a reader of the public record can verify.

02

How each topic is scored

Scale A · 0–3

A four-rung ordinal, applied 20 times per company, once to each topic in the framework. Every bar and mean on the Findings and Sector tabs is built from it. "Owned" throughout this site means a topic reached rung 2 or rung 3.

weaker evidencestronger
Why rung 3 is asymmetric For the two risk-oversight domains, rung 3 requires a named executive plus a stated cadence reporting to a board body. For the four value domains cadence is the wrong test: what matters is not how often the board is briefed but whether it decides anything, so rung 3 there requires a decision the board takes over investments, M&A, portfolio or programs.
03

How each company is classified

Scale B · 1–4

A separate instrument, and the one most often confused with the scoring ladder above. This is a single classification for the whole board, made once per company from structural evidence in the filing, not a score, not an average of the topic scores, and on a different range. It drives the "By maturity band" cut and nothing else on this site.

Telling the two apart Scale A runs 0–3 and fires 20 times per company, once per topic. Scale B runs 1–4 and fires once per company, for the board as a whole. A company classified at maturity 3 still carries 20 separate topic scores on scale A.
Numbering changed on 27 Jul 2026 This scale was consolidated from 1–5 to 1–4 after the original level 1 ("Ad hoc") failed to fire on any of 472 coded rows: every company that files a proxy allocates cyber oversight somewhere, so the observed floor was always the second rung. The retired level was removed and the rest renumbered down by one. Nothing was re-scored and no company moved relative to any other. Any project document dated before 27 Jul 2026 uses the old 1–5 numbering.
04

Framework & sources

The framework

Six domains, 20 topics. Two are risk oversight, protecting existing value. Four are value creation, generating future value. The gap reported throughout is the difference between a company's mean across those two groups.

Sources, in priority order

Where a company appears in more than one source, the stronger evidence wins.

The largest single gap Charters state a committee's actual remit, and are the documented fix for the value-creation floor. Coverage is …. Value-creation domains are systematically understated for every company without one.
05

Sample, exclusions & verification

The sample

…

Not a population estimate A census of large-cap U.S. filers with machine-readable disclosure, not a random sample of American companies. Do not extrapolate to private companies, smaller filers, or non-U.S. issuers.

Exclusions, disclosed

…

These are extraction failures, not governance findings. The clearest case is the banking incorporation-by-reference pattern, where Item 1C is a cross-reference index containing no scoreable sentences. Averaging those in would have made the headline partly a statement about filing format rather than about board behaviour.

Human verification

…

What a charter changes

Where a charter was located and read, the picture changes materially: the single biggest reason to treat the value-creation figures as a floor rather than an estimate.

06

Five things that would change these numbers

Stated up front rather than in an appendix, because each one has a known direction and a known size.

01 · Disclosure is a proxy for behaviour Absence of evidence in a filing is not evidence of absence of oversight. The bias is one-way and the direction is known: every score on this site is a floor.
02 · Charter coverage Where a charter was read, mean value-creation score is … against … where none was. With coverage at …, the value-creation figures are the least settled numbers here.
03 · Level 1 is the least reliable tier Soft context-inheritance matches and false positives concentrate at level 1, so it is excluded from every breadth figure and reported as a separate band instead.
04 · Inter-rater reliability is not yet established A blind re-code of a subsample against a 0.67 alpha gate is designed and outstanding. Until it clears, the shape of the distribution is the claim; individual scores are not.
05 · The structure comparison is confounded Standing-committee companies have far higher charter coverage than existing-committee companies, so part of their apparent advantage is document access rather than governance. Flagged in place on the Sector & structure tab. Do not publish that comparison as causal until coverage is equalised.
07

Reproducibility

Every score traces to a quoted sentence and a filing URL. The company-level record, score, quoted evidence, note, source and filing link for all 20 topics, is retained in full and is available in the explorer for review purposes, marked unverified. Nothing on the public tabs is computed by hand; the page is generated from the scored dataset on each build, so the figures cannot drift from the underlying workbook without the build failing.

Company-level detail is unverified

The aggregate findings on this site are the published research. The per-company view behind this screen is an internal audit tool, kept so that any individual read can be checked against its source text. It is not a rating and is not intended for citation.

  • Scores are machine-drafted; only part of the sample carries a completed human review.
  • Known extraction failures are present and flagged inline rather than removed.
  • A low score frequently means thin disclosure, not weak governance.
  • Inter-rater reliability for these scores has not yet been established.
Unverified working data. Individual company scores must not be quoted or published.
Anchors. 0 absent. 1 named in a board context. 2 a board body owns it. 3 process evidence: for the two risk domains a named executive plus a stated cadence to a board body; for the four value-creation domains a decision the board takes over investments, M&A, portfolio or programs.

Reading the sources. Every company record links to the filings it was scored from. Where a charter has not been retrieved the record says so, and the value-creation domains for that company should be read as a floor rather than a finding: charters carry the mandate language that proxies summarise away.
